claim: p97/VCP is an essential, abundant AAA+ ATPase that is conserved throughout eukaryotes.
source: p97/VCP is an essential, abundant AAA+ ATPase that is conserved throughout eukaryotes, with central functions in diverse processes ranging from protein degradation to DNA damage repair and membrane fusion.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge about p97/VCP characteristics.

claim: p97/VCP has central functions in diverse processes ranging from protein degradation to DNA damage repair and membrane fusion.
source: p97/VCP is an essential, abundant AAA+ ATPase that is conserved throughout eukaryotes, with central functions in diverse processes ranging from protein degradation to DNA damage repair and membrane fusion.
evidence: This is supported by established scientific knowledge and citations throughout the manuscript.

claim: p97 has been implicated in the etiology of degenerative diseases and in cancer.
source: p97 has been implicated in the etiology of degenerative diseases and in cancer.
evidence: This is supported by citations and established knowledge in the field.

claim: Disease-causing mutations in p97 deregulate dynamics of the N-terminal domain that binds adaptor proteins involved in controlling p97 function.
source: Using Nuclear Magnetic Resonance spectroscopy we reveal how disease-causing mutations in p97 deregulate dynamics of the N-terminal domain that binds adaptor proteins involved in controlling p97 function.
evidence: This is a primary finding of the study supported by NMR data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Mutations shift the ADP-bound form of the enzyme towards an ATP-like state in a manner that correlates with disease severity.
source: Our results provide a molecular basis for understanding how malfunction occurs whereby mutations shift the ADP-bound form of the enzyme towards an ATP-like state in a manner that correlates with disease severity.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data showing chemical shift changes and correlation with disease severity metrics.

claim: This deregulation interferes with the two-pronged binding of an adaptor that affects p97 function in lysosomal degradation of substrates.
source: This deregulation interferes with the two-pronged binding of an adaptor that affects p97 function in lysosomal degradation of substrates.
evidence: This is supported by NMR binding studies with UBXD1 adaptor protein.

claim: Subtle structural changes propagate from mutation sites to regions distal in space, defining allosteric networks that facilitate inter-domain communication.
source: Subtle structural changes propagate from mutation sites to regions distal in space, defining allosteric networks that facilitate inter-domain communication, with potential implications for modulation of enzyme activity by drug molecules.
evidence: This is supported by chemical shift perturbation data showing long-range effects of mutations.

claim: The valosin containing protein (VCP) or p97 is a highly conserved enzyme in mammalian cells, with orthologues in yeast (Cdc48), in flies (TER94) and in archaea (VAT).
source: The valosin containing protein (VCP) or p97 is a highly conserved enzyme in mammalian cells, with orthologues in yeast (Cdc48), in flies (TER94) and in archaea (VAT) (Rabouille et al., 1995).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rabouille et al., 1995.

claim: p97 is involved in membrane fusion.
source: It is involved in various processes in the cell (Figure 1A) including membrane fusion (Rabouille et al., 1995), chromatin-associated functions (Moreno et al., 2014; Dantuma and Hoppe, 2012), cell cycle progression (Cao et al., 2003), and apoptosis (Madeo et al., 1997) and it is active in proteasomal degradation (Richly et al., 2005), autophagy (Ju et al., 2009; Buchan et al., 2013), and in endosomal pathways (Ritz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Rabouille et al., 1995 and Figure 1A.

claim: p97 is involved in chromatin-associated functions.
source: It is involved in various processes in the cell (Figure 1A) including membrane fusion (Rabouille et al., 1995), chromatin-associated functions (Moreno et al., 2014; Dantuma and Hoppe, 2012), cell cycle progression (Cao et al., 2003), and apoptosis (Madeo et al., 1997) and it is active in proteasomal degradation (Richly et al., 2005), autophagy (Ju et al., 2009; Buchan et al., 2013), and in endosomal pathways (Ritz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moreno et al., 2014 and Dantuma and Hoppe, 2012.

claim: p97 is involved in cell cycle progression.
source: It is involved in various processes in the cell (Figure 1A) including membrane fusion (Rabouille et al., 1995), chromatin-associated functions (Moreno et al., 2014; Dantuma and Hoppe, 2012), cell cycle progression (Cao et al., 2003), and apoptosis (Madeo et al., 1997) and it is active in proteasomal degradation (Richly et al., 2005), autophagy (Ju et al., 2009; Buchan et al., 2013), and in endosomal pathways (Ritz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Cao et al., 2003.

claim: p97 is involved in apoptosis.
source: It is involved in various processes in the cell (Figure 1A) including membrane fusion (Rabouille et al., 1995), chromatin-associated functions (Moreno et al., 2014; Dantuma and Hoppe, 2012), cell cycle progression (Cao et al., 2003), and apoptosis (Madeo et al., 1997) and it is active in proteasomal degradation (Richly et al., 2005), autophagy (Ju et al., 2009; Buchan et al., 2013), and in endosomal pathways (Ritz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Madeo et al., 1997.

claim: p97 is active in proteasomal degradation.
source: It is involved in various processes in the cell (Figure 1A) including membrane fusion (Rabouille et al., 1995), chromatin-associated functions (Moreno et al., 2014; Dantuma and Hoppe, 2012), cell cycle progression (Cao et al., 2003), and apoptosis (Madeo et al., 1997) and it is active in proteasomal degradation (Richly et al., 2005), autophagy (Ju et al., 2009; Buchan et al., 2013), and in endosomal pathways (Ritz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Richly et al., 2005.

claim: p97 is active in autophagy.
source: It is involved in various processes in the cell (Figure 1A) including membrane fusion (Rabouille et al., 1995), chromatin-associated functions (Moreno et al., 2014; Dantuma and Hoppe, 2012), cell cycle progression (Cao et al., 2003), and apoptosis (Madeo et al., 1997) and it is active in proteasomal degradation (Richly et al., 2005), autophagy (Ju et al., 2009; Buchan et al., 2013), and in endosomal pathways (Ritz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ju et al., 2009 and Buchan et al., 2013.

claim: p97 is active in endosomal pathways.
source: It is involved in various processes in the cell (Figure 1A) including membrane fusion (Rabouille et al., 1995), chromatin-associated functions (Moreno et al., 2014; Dantuma and Hoppe, 2012), cell cycle progression (Cao et al., 2003), and apoptosis (Madeo et al., 1997) and it is active in proteasomal degradation (Richly et al., 2005), autophagy (Ju et al., 2009; Buchan et al., 2013), and in endosomal pathways (Ritz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ritz et al., 2011.

claim: The involvement of p97 in all major proteolysis pathways makes it a central player in cellular homeostasis.
source: The involvement of p97 in all major proteolysis pathways makes it a central player in cellular homeostasis (Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Meyer et al., 2012.

claim: p97 is a 540 kDa homo-hexamer (6x89 kDa).
source: p97 is a 540 kDa homo-hexamer (6x89 kDa) with each monomer comprising an N-terminal domain (NTD) and a pair of ATPase domains, D1 and D2, arranged in primary sequence as NTD-D1-D2.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about p97.

claim: Each p97 monomer comprises an N-terminal domain (NTD) and a pair of ATPase domains, D1 and D2, arranged in primary sequence as NTD-D1-D2.
source: p97 is a 540 kDa homo-hexamer (6x89 kDa) with each monomer comprising an N-terminal domain (NTD) and a pair of ATPase domains, D1 and D2, arranged in primary sequence as NTD-D1-D2.
evidence: This is established structural knowledge about p97.

claim: Both D1 and D2 are organized as rings that stack coaxially, with the NTD located at the periphery of the D1 ring.
source: Both D1 and D2 are organized as rings that stack coaxially, with the NTD located at the periphery of the D1 ring (DeLaBarre and Brunger, 2003) (Figure 1B,C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to DeLaBarre and Brunger, 2003 and Figure 1B,C.

claim: p97 converts the energy obtained via ATP hydrolysis to remove substrates from complexes or membranes and to structurally remodel or unfold them.
source: p97 converts the energy obtained via ATP hydrolysis to remove substrates from complexes or membranes and to structurally remodel or unfold them (Barthelme and Sauer, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Barthelme and Sauer, 2016.

claim: p97's diverse activities result from various cofactors that recruit it to specific functions.
source: Its diverse activities result from various cofactors that recruit it to specific functions (Buchberger et al., 2015), with more than 40 adaptors discovered in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Buchberger et al., 2015.

claim: More than 40 adaptors have been discovered in mammalian cells for p97.
source: Its diverse activities result from various cofactors that recruit it to specific functions (Buchberger et al., 2015), with more than 40 adaptors discovered in mammalian cells.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Buchberger et al., 2015.

claim: Many p97 adaptors contain highly conserved p97 binding domains such as UBX and VIM.
source: Many of these contain highly conserved p97 binding domains such as UBX (Buchberger et al., 2001) and VIM (Stapf et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Buchberger et al., 2001 and Stapf et al., 2011.

claim: p97 deletion results in early embryonic lethality.
source: Given its prominent role in the eukaryotic cell, p97 misfunction is associated with human disease. While p97 deletion results in early embryonic lethality (Müller et al., 2007), a series of missense mutations lead to very specific malfunctions in protein homeostasis linked to degenerative disorders (Watts et al., 2004), among them Inclusion Body Myopathy associated with Paget disease of the bone and Frontotemporal Dementia (IBMPFD), a lethal autosomal dominant disorder with onset in midlife.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Müller et al., 2007.

claim: A series of missense mutations in p97 lead to very specific malfunctions in protein homeostasis linked to degenerative disorders.
source: While p97 deletion results in early embryonic lethality (Müller et al., 2007), a series of missense mutations lead to very specific malfunctions in protein homeostasis linked to degenerative disorders (Watts et al., 2004), among them Inclusion Body Myopathy associated with Paget disease of the bone and Frontotemporal Dementia (IBMPFD), a lethal autosomal dominant disorder with onset in midlife.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Watts et al., 2004.

claim: IBMPFD is a lethal autosomal dominant disorder with onset in midlife.
source: While p97 deletion results in early embryonic lethality (Müller et al., 2007), a series of missense mutations lead to very specific malfunctions in protein homeostasis linked to degenerative disorders (Watts et al., 2004), among them Inclusion Body Myopathy associated with Paget disease of the bone and Frontotemporal Dementia (IBMPFD), a lethal autosomal dominant disorder with onset in midlife.
evidence: This is established clinical knowledge about IBMPFD.

claim: IBMPFD mutations mostly occur at the NTD-D1 interface or in the linker region between these domains.
source: These mutations, mostly occurring at the NTD-D1 interface or in the linker region between these domains (Figure 2), also lead to an increased occurrence of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Johnson et al., 2011) and of familial Parkinson's disease (Chan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by Figure 2 showing mutation locations.

claim: IBMPFD mutations lead to an increased occurrence of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis.
source: These mutations, mostly occurring at the NTD-D1 interface or in the linker region between these domains (Figure 2), also lead to an increased occurrence of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Johnson et al., 2011) and of familial Parkinson's disease (Chan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Johnson et al., 2011.

claim: IBMPFD mutations lead to an increased occurrence of familial Parkinson's disease.
source: These mutations, mostly occurring at the NTD-D1 interface or in the linker region between these domains (Figure 2), also lead to an increased occurrence of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (Johnson et al., 2011) and of familial Parkinson's disease (Chan et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Chan et al., 2012.

claim: The mobility of the NTD is of particular functional relevance.
source: Of particular functional relevance is the mobility of the NTD, which has been shown to undergo large displacements during the nucleotide cycle (Tang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tang et al., 2010.

claim: The NTD undergoes large displacements during the nucleotide cycle.
source: Of particular functional relevance is the mobility of the NTD, which has been shown to undergo large displacements during the nucleotide cycle (Tang et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tang et al., 2010.

claim: NTDs are the major binding sites for cofactors along with substrates.
source: NTDs are the major binding sites for cofactors along with substrates and cross-linking NTD to D1 via disulfides abrogates all ATPase activity (both in D1 and in D2) (Niwa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Niwa et al., 2012.

claim: Cross-linking NTD to D1 via disulfides abrogates all ATPase activity (both in D1 and in D2).
source: NTDs are the major binding sites for cofactors along with substrates and cross-linking NTD to D1 via disulfides abrogates all ATPase activity (both in D1 and in D2) (Niwa et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Niwa et al., 2012.

claim: NTD is coplanar relative to D1 in both wild-type and disease mutants of p97-ADP (down state).
source: Crystallographic studies (Tang et al., 2010) conducted on a truncated form of p97 comprising NTD and D1 show that NTD is coplanar relative to D1 in both wild-type (wt) and disease mutants of p97-ADP (referred to in what follows as the down state, Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B) and elevated relative to D1 in p97-ATPγS disease mutants (up state, Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tang et al., 2010 and Figures 1B and 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: NTD is elevated relative to D1 in p97-ATPγS disease mutants (up state).
source: Crystallographic studies (Tang et al., 2010) conducted on a truncated form of p97 comprising NTD and D1 show that NTD is coplanar relative to D1 in both wild-type (wt) and disease mutants of p97-ADP (referred to in what follows as the down state, Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B) and elevated relative to D1 in p97-ATPγS disease mutants (up state, Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tang et al., 2010 and Figures 1C and 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The nucleotide state in D1, but not in D2, determines the NTD up/down conformation.
source: Complementary static pictures recently obtained from electron microscopy on full-length wt p97 (22) confirm that the nucleotide state in D1, but not in D2, determines the NTD up/down conformation and establish that the up-conformation in the ATPγS state is not an anomaly of the disease mutants but also found in wt protein.
evidence: This is supported by citation (22) referring to electron microscopy studies.

claim: The up-conformation in the ATPγS state is not an anomaly of the disease mutants but also found in wt protein.
source: Complementary static pictures recently obtained from electron microscopy on full-length wt p97 (22) confirm that the nucleotide state in D1, but not in D2, determines the NTD up/down conformation and establish that the up-conformation in the ATPγS state is not an anomaly of the disease mutants but also found in wt protein.
evidence: This is supported by citation (22) referring to electron microscopy studies.

claim: Well-resolved resonances in 13C-1H HMQC spectra of ILVM-13CH3-ND1Lp97 and full length p97 (6*89 kDa) labeled in the same manner are superimposable.
source: Well-resolved resonances in 13C-1H HMQC spectra of ILVM-13CH3-ND1Lp97 and full length p97 (6*89 kDa) labeled in the same manner are superimposable (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), establishing that ND1Lp97 is a good model system for structural studies.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: ND1Lp97 is a good model system for structural studies of p97.
source: Well-resolved resonances in 13C-1H HMQC spectra of ILVM-13CH3-ND1Lp97 and full length p97 (6*89 kDa) labeled in the same manner are superimposable (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), establishing that ND1Lp97 is a good model system for structural studies.
evidence: This is inferred from the superimposable NMR spectra shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Substantial changes in spectra are noted for ND1Lp97 as a function of nucleotide (ADP or ATPγS).
source: Substantial changes in spectra are noted for ND1Lp97 as a function of nucleotide (ADP or ATPγS) that are detected across the entire protein, consistent with a major rearrangement of the NTD from up to down as ATP is converted to ADP (Tang et al., 2010; Banerjee et al., 2016), Figure 3, Figure 3—figure supplement 2.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 3 and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Out of more than 20 different disease sites that have been reported to date in humans, 7 have been chosen for NMR analysis.
source: Out of more than 20 different disease sites that have been reported to date in humans (Darvish et al., 2004; Mehta et al., 2013; Evangelista et al., 2016), 7 have been chosen for NMR analysis, Figure 2A.
evidence: This is supported by citations and Figure 2A showing the selected mutation sites.

claim: The ATPγS state, ND1Lp97-ATPγS, is little affected by the mutations considered, beyond the immediate site of substitution.
source: The ATPγS state, ND1Lp97-ATPγS, is little affected by the mutations considered, beyond the immediate site of substitution, as can be seen in a comparison of spectra recorded on wt and R95G ND1Lp97 samples (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The disease mutants sample similar conformations as the wt protein in the ATPγS-bound form.
source: Because chemical shifts are sensitive probes of structure this result strongly suggests that the disease mutants sample similar conformations as the wt protein in the ATPγS-bound form.
evidence: This is inferred from the similar chemical shifts observed in NMR spectra.

claim: Substantial changes are observed for many methyl probes in ND1Lp97-ADP, including those in the NTD, N-D1 linker and D1 regions.
source: In contrast, substantial changes are observed for many methyl probes in ND1Lp97-ADP, including those in the NTD, N-D1 linker and D1 regions.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data showing chemical shift changes.

claim: Changes in chemical shifts generally titrate with mutation in a linear fashion.
source: These changes in chemical shifts generally titrate with mutation in a linear fashion, (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B), not withstanding the methyl groups close to the sites of mutation or nucleotide binding whose positions can be perturbed simply by the substitution or the presence of ADP/ATP, respectively.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Mutations lead to a gradual conversion to a more ATP-like conformation despite the absence of ATP.
source: Thus, although mutations are localized to different domains and can be distant in space from each other, their impact on the structure and dynamics of ND1Lp97-ADP can be described in terms of a simple, unifying model whereby mutations lead to a gradual conversion to a more ATP-like conformation (red to black in Figure 4B, despite the absence of ATP), consistent with a gradual upward movement of the NTD.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: The CSPs for both ND1Lp97 and full-length p97 are identical.
source: Figure 4C shows the superposition of regions of 13C-1H HMQC spectra recorded of both wt and R95G variants of ND1Lp97-ADP and full-length p97-ADP. It is clear that the CSPs for both ND1Lp97 and full-length p97 are identical so that the upwards movement of the NTD upon introduction of disease mutations, characterized in ND1Lp97-ADP, is also observed in the intact molecule.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The upwards movement of the NTD upon introduction of disease mutations, characterized in ND1Lp97-ADP, is also observed in the intact molecule.
source: It is clear that the CSPs for both ND1Lp97 and full-length p97 are identical so that the upwards movement of the NTD upon introduction of disease mutations, characterized in ND1Lp97-ADP, is also observed in the intact molecule.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data comparing ND1Lp97 and full-length p97.

claim: The NTD is not static in p97-ADP, but rather exchanges rapidly between up/down states.
source: Thus, unlike the picture from X-ray studies of disease mutants, our NMR results establish that the NTD is not static in p97-ADP, but rather exchanges rapidly between up/down states, with the relative mixture of each state changing with mutation.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by NMR data showing chemical shift changes and dynamics measurements.

claim: The exchange rate between up/down NTD states is estimated to be greater than 2000 s−1.
source: The exchange rate is estimated to be greater than 2000 s−1, based on the chemical shift differences between ADP and ATPγS-bound states, as measured for the I189 Cδ1 that has the largest CSPs.
evidence: This is calculated from NMR chemical shift data.

claim: CSPs extend from the site of mutation to the nucleotide-binding region and beyond to the p97 central pore, identifying potential allosteric pathways of communication throughout the protein.
source: CSPs extend from the site of mutation (yellow) to the nucleotide-binding region and beyond to the p97 central pore, identifying potential allosteric pathways of communication throughout the protein (see Discussion).
evidence: This is supported by NMR chemical shift perturbation data mapped onto the structure.

claim: The 22 residues in ND1Lp97 that are mutated in IBMPFD disease patients localize to regions with large CSPs.
source: The 22 residues in ND1Lp97 that are mutated in IBMPFD disease patients are shown in stick representation in red in Figure 5B. These mutation sites localize to regions with large CSPs.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Regions of the NTD that are associated with UBX and VIM domain binding are not perturbed by the disease mutations.
source: Notably, regions of the NTD that are associated with UBX and VIM domain binding (see below) are not perturbed by the disease mutations (no CSPs).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data showing no chemical shift perturbations in these regions.

claim: Correlation times of 91 ± 3 ns and 68 ± 2 ns were determined for ADP and ATPγS bound wt states, respectively.
source: Correlation times of 91 ± 3 ns and 68 ± 2 ns were determined for ADP and ATPγS bound wt states, respectively, while a value of 13 ns was measured for the isolated NTD.
evidence: This is supported by NMR relaxation measurements.

claim: A value of 13 ns was measured for the isolated NTD.
source: Correlation times of 91 ± 3 ns and 68 ± 2 ns were determined for ADP and ATPγS bound wt states, respectively, while a value of 13 ns was measured for the isolated NTD.
evidence: This is supported by NMR relaxation measurements.

claim: The NTD is only partially docked to D1, with more motional freedom in p97-ATPγS.
source: This implies that the NTD is only partially docked to D1, as expected on the basis of X-ray and cryo-EM models of p97 (20, 22), with more motional freedom in p97-ATPγS.
evidence: This is inferred from NMR correlation time measurements and supported by citations to structural studies.

claim: A value of τc = 100 ± 3 ns was obtained for an intra-protomer cross-linked variant that tethers the NTD to D1.
source: A value of τc = 100 ± 3 ns was obtained for an intra-protomer cross-linked variant that tethers the NTD to D1 (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is supported by NMR relaxation measurements shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The NTD tumbling time (τc) decreases (mobility increases) as the percentage of NTD in the up conformation grows.
source: Values of pU for a range of disease mutants are listed in Figure 6B (purple) along with τc values (blue), with τc decreasing (mobility increasing) as the percentage of NTD in the up conformation grows, Figure 6C.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 6B and 6C.

claim: The chemical shift and relaxation data provide strong evidence that the NTDs are dynamic, rapidly interconverting between up/down conformers.
source: Both the chemical shift and relaxation data provide strong evidence that the NTDs are dynamic, rapidly interconverting between up/down conformers.
evidence: This is supported by NMR chemical shift and relaxation data.

claim: The 13C-1H HMQC spectrum of R95G,R155C,N387C ND1Lp97-ADP under oxidizing conditions shows large CSPs for I146 and I189, consistent with disulfide bond formation.
source: The 13C-1H HMQC spectrum of R95G,R155C,N387C ND1Lp97-ADP, Figure 6D, under oxidizing conditions shows large CSPs for I146 and I189, consistent with disulfide bond formation.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: The disease mutants affect the up/down equilibrium in p97-ADP, with the NTD almost entirely up in the R95G/T262A double mutant, similar to the ATPγS-conformation.
source: Taken together our data indicate that the disease mutants affect the up/down equilibrium in p97-ADP, with the NTD almost entirely up in the R95G/T262A double mutant, similar to the ATPγS-conformation (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The UBXD1 adaptor protein is abundant in neuronal cells.
source: The UBXD1 adaptor protein is abundant in neuronal cells (Madsen et al., 2008; Nagahama et al., 2009) and a complex with p97 binds to the plasma membrane protein caveolin-1, mediating sorting of ubiquitylated cargo in endosomal degradation (Ritz et al., 2011) (Figure 1A, region highlighted in the orange square).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Madsen et al., 2008 and Nagahama et al., 2009.

claim: A complex of UBXD1 with p97 binds to the plasma membrane protein caveolin-1, mediating sorting of ubiquitylated cargo in endosomal degradation.
source: The UBXD1 adaptor protein is abundant in neuronal cells (Madsen et al., 2008; Nagahama et al., 2009) and a complex with p97 binds to the plasma membrane protein caveolin-1, mediating sorting of ubiquitylated cargo in endosomal degradation (Ritz et al., 2011) (Figure 1A, region highlighted in the orange square).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ritz et al., 2011.

claim: The UBXD1-p97 complex is specifically disrupted in disease-associated mutations and function is impaired.
source: Importantly, the UBXD1-p97 complex is specifically disrupted in disease-associated mutations and function is impaired (Ritz et al., 2011) but the molecular details underlying this disruption are not understood.
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ritz et al., 2011.

claim: The VIM domain of UBXD1 is localized to the canonical VIM/UBX binding site on the NTD.
source: An elegant biophysical study of the isolated NTD with the N-terminal portion of UBXD1 (UBXD1-N, residues 1–133, Figure 7A) (Trusch et al., 2015) shows an interaction involving VIM (residues 52–63) that is localized to the canonical VIM/UBX binding site on the NTD (Stapf et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Trusch et al., 2015 and Stapf et al., 2011.

claim: The N-terminus of UBXD1 may engage the NTD-D1 interface and NTD-D1 linker, where disease mutations occur.
source: Moreover, the authors suggest that the N-terminus of UBXD1 may engage the NTD-D1 interface and NTD-D1 linker, where disease mutations occur, and hypothesize that this secondary interaction may favor a more compact conformation of p97.
evidence: This is a hypothesis from a cited study (Trusch et al., 2015).

claim: Binding of UBXD1-N causes small shifts to I146 and I189 of the wt protein that are consistent with locking the NTD in the down conformation.
source: Binding of UBXD1-N causes small shifts to I146 and I189 of the wt protein (Figure 7B) that are consistent with locking the NTD in the down conformation, as observed upon chemical cross-linking (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 7B and comparison with Figure 6E.

claim: A Kd value of 22 ± 2 µM for the VIM-NTD interaction is calculated for wt p97.
source: Larger shifts are observed for V68 and I175 that report on VIM binding, from which a Kd value of 22 ± 2 µM for the VIM-NTD interaction is calculated (see Materials and methods Figure 7—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is calculated from NMR titration data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3.

claim: Studies of R155H and N387H mutants show that two-pronged binding involving VIM and H1/H2 occurs partially but that a complete down conformation is not obtained with a 3-fold excess of adaptor over p97 protomer.
source: Studies of R155H and N387H mutants of ND1Lp97-ADP that mildly perturb the up/down equilibrium (Figure 7C, Figure 7—figure supplement 2D) show that two-pronged binding involving VIM and H1/H2 occurs partially but that a complete down conformation is not obtained with a 3-fold excess of adaptor over p97 protomer (compare dashed and solid arrows that correspond to movements for peaks from wt and mutant p97, respectively).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 7—figure supplement 2D.

claim: A Kd value of ~80 µM is obtained for the VIM-NTD interaction in mild disease mutants.
source: A Kd value of ~80 µM is obtained for the VIM-NTD interaction in this class of mild disease mutants.
evidence: This is calculated from NMR data.

claim: While the VIM domain weakly binds to the NTD of the strong mutants R95G and R155P ND1Lp97-ADP (Kd ~ 200 µM), there is no binding of H1/H2 and no shift in the conformational equilibrium towards the down state.
source: Notably, while the VIM domain weakly binds to the NTD of the strong mutants R95G and R155P ND1Lp97-ADP, Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2E, (Kd ~ 200 µM, see Materials and methods) there is no binding of H1/H2 and no shift in the conformational equilibrium towards the down state, as evidenced by a lack of CSPs for I146 and I189 (3:1 UBXD1-N:p97 monomer ratio).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Very similar CSPs were obtained for wt and R95G proteins upon binding full-length p47.
source: Very similar CSPs were further obtained for wt and R95G proteins upon binding full-length p47 (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C), which interacts as a trimer (Beuron et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: p47 interacts with p97 as a trimer.
source: Very similar CSPs were further obtained for wt and R95G proteins upon binding full-length p47 (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C), which interacts as a trimer (Beuron et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Beuron et al., 2006.

claim: The CSPs upon binding p47 are distinct both in magnitude and in direction from those that result from perturbation to the NTP up/down equilibrium.
source: Notably, the CSPs upon binding p47 are distinct both in magnitude and in direction from those that result from perturbation to the NTP up/down equilibrium (Figure 8A, Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 8A and Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Binding of p47 occurs at two sites, with one region corresponding to the canonical UBX binding site of the NTD and a second unique site on the NTD that engages the SHP domain of p47.
source: Binding occurs at two sites, with one region corresponding to the canonical UBX binding site of the NTD (yellow), as observed for the binding of the VIM domain of UBXD1-N. A second unique site on the NTD (purple) is also involved in binding that has been shown in a previous structural study to engage the SHP domain of p47 (Hänzelmann et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data and citation to Hänzelmann et al., 2016.

claim: The p47-p97 interaction is not significantly perturbed by disease mutations.
source: Unlike the second site for UBXD1-N binding that bridges the NTD and D1 domains, the site of engagement of SHP does not, so that it is not surprising that the p47-p97 interaction is not significantly perturbed by disease mutations.
evidence: This is inferred from NMR data showing similar binding for wt and mutant p97.

claim: IBMPFD disease mutants affect lysosome-related functions but not others, such as endoplasmic reticulum associated degradation and Golgi membrane fusion.
source: It is notable that IBMPFD disease mutants affect lysosome-related functions but not others, such as endoplasmic reticulum associated degradation and Golgi membrane fusion (Tresse et al., 2010; Meyer and Weihl, 2014; Johnson et al., 2015) (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tresse et al., 2010, Meyer and Weihl, 2014, and Johnson et al., 2015.

claim: The mild disease mutants introduce only subtle changes to the equilibrium, with R155H and N387H mutations shifting the NTD equilibrium from 0% up to ~15% up in p97-ADP.
source: The answer partly lies in the fact that the mild disease mutants introduce only subtle changes to the equilibrium, with R155H and N387H mutations shifting the NTD equilibrium from 0% up to ~15% up in p97-ADP, for example.
evidence: This is calculated from NMR data.

claim: The differences in free energies between the up and down conformations are relatively small, with △Gup/down(R155H) ~ 1200 cal/mol and △Gup/down(R95G) ~ 200 cal/mol.
source: Moreover the differences in free energies between the up and down conformations are relatively small, with △Gup/down(R155H) ~ 1200 cal/mol and △Gup/down(R95G) ~ 200 cal/mol based on the measured pU values (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is calculated from NMR data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Crystal structures of weak disease mutants in the ADP state (R155H, L198W) have been published and all show the down NTD conformation, as for the wt.
source: For example, while crystal structures of weak disease mutants in the ADP state (R155H, L198W) have been published and all show the down NTD conformation, as for the wt, structures of strong mutants such as R95G, R155C/P in the ADP state (△Gup/down~0 cal/mol) have not been reported.
evidence: This is based on published crystallographic studies.

claim: Structures of strong mutants such as R95G, R155C/P in the ADP state have not been reported.
source: For example, while crystal structures of weak disease mutants in the ADP state (R155H, L198W) have been published and all show the down NTD conformation, as for the wt, structures of strong mutants such as R95G, R155C/P in the ADP state (△Gup/down~0 cal/mol) have not been reported.
evidence: This is based on the absence of such structures in the literature.

claim: On an atomic scale, only localized changes were observed in the crystal structures of mutants of p97-ADP relative to the wt conformation.
source: On an atomic scale, only localized changes were observed in the crystal structures of mutants of p97-ADP relative to the wt conformation (Tang et al., 2010; Tang and Xia, 2013; Tang and Xia, 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tang et al., 2010, Tang and Xia, 2013, and Tang and Xia, 2016.

claim: The sidechain of R359, which serves as a sensor of the nucleotide state of an adjacent protomer, is slightly shifted in disease mutants and this shift is thought to lead to a destabilization of the ADP state.
source: For example, the sidechain of R359, which serves as a sensor of the nucleotide state of an adjacent protomer, is slightly shifted and this shift is thought to lead to a destabilization of the ADP state in mutants.
evidence: This is based on crystallographic observations and interpretation.

claim: The sidechain orientation of F360 differs between ADP states of wt and disease mutants.
source: Moreover, the sidechain orientation of F360 differs between ADP states of wt and disease mutants (Tang and Xia, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Tang and Xia, 2013.

claim: Structural differences in disease mutants are thought to result in defective communication between subunits in mutant p97 molecules.
source: Together, these structural differences are thought to result in defective communication between subunits in mutant p97 molcules.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on structural observations.

claim: Beyond the primary defect in UBXD1 binding, altered cofactor interactions have been reported in a number of studies, including those of p47, p37, Ufd1-Npl4, E4B and ataxin-3.
source: Beyond the primary defect in UBXD1 binding (Ritz et al., 2011), altered cofactor interactions have been reported in a number of studies, including those of p47, p37, Ufd1-Npl4, E4B and ataxin-3 (41, 53, 54).
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Changes in adaptor interactions are expected whenever adaptors bind differentially to the up and down conformations of the NTD.
source: Due to the NTD conformational equilibrium shift in disease mutants, changes in interactions are expected whenever adaptors bind differentially to the up and down conformations of the NTD, which are characteristic of ATP and ADP states of wt p97, respectively.
evidence: This is inferred from the NMR data showing conformational equilibrium shifts.

claim: Intact or even increased p47 binding of mutants has been detected.
source: In these studies intact or even increased p47 binding of mutants has been detected (Fernández-Sáiz and Buchberger, 2010; Bulfer et al., 2016) and no differences in ATP hydrolysis kinetics between wt and disease mutant p97-p47 complexes in the limit of saturated binding have been observed (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Fernández-Sáiz and Buchberger, 2010 and Bulfer et al., 2016.

claim: No differences in ATP hydrolysis kinetics between wt and disease mutant p97-p47 complexes in the limit of saturated binding have been observed.
source: In these studies intact or even increased p47 binding of mutants has been detected (Fernández-Sáiz and Buchberger, 2010; Bulfer et al., 2016) and no differences in ATP hydrolysis kinetics between wt and disease mutant p97-p47 complexes in the limit of saturated binding have been observed (Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2015.

claim: The p97-p47 complex is formed analogously in wt and disease mutants.
source: They do establish, however, that the p97-p47 complex is formed analogously in wt and disease mutants (Figure 8A), and, unique to the NMR, that the skewed NTD conformational equilibrium found in disease mutants of p97-ADP is conserved in the p47 bound complex.
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The skewed NTD conformational equilibrium found in disease mutants of p97-ADP is conserved in the p47 bound complex.
source: They do establish, however, that the p97-p47 complex is formed analogously in wt and disease mutants (Figure 8A), and, unique to the NMR, that the skewed NTD conformational equilibrium found in disease mutants of p97-ADP is conserved in the p47 bound complex.
evidence: This is a finding unique to the NMR studies presented.

claim: Disease mutations slightly decrease the affinity of D1 for ADP (by factors between 2–4) but not for ATP.
source: In general, the literature consensus is that disease mutations slightly decrease the affinity of D1 for ADP (by factors between 2–4) but not for ATP, while increasing the ADP release rate from D1 by approximately 2-fold (Tang et al., 2010; Tang and Xia, 2013; Bulfer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on literature consensus supported by citations.

claim: Disease mutations increase the ADP release rate from D1 by approximately 2-fold.
source: In general, the literature consensus is that disease mutations slightly decrease the affinity of D1 for ADP (by factors between 2–4) but not for ATP, while increasing the ADP release rate from D1 by approximately 2-fold (Tang et al., 2010; Tang and Xia, 2013; Bulfer et al., 2016).
evidence: This is based on literature consensus supported by citations.

claim: There is no simple correlation between biophysical properties of various disease mutants and either perturbation of the NTD conformational equilibrium or empirical disease severity in patients.
source: We have observed no simple correlation between biophysical properties of various disease mutants and either perturbation of the NTD conformational equilibrium or empirical disease severity in patients.
evidence: This is based on analysis of the data presented in the study.

claim: ATPase activities of disease mutants were reported to be normal in some and elevated in other studies but not in a manner that correlates with disease severity.
source: As an example, ATPase activities of disease mutants were reported to be normal in some (Fernández-Sáiz and Buchberger, 2010) and elevated in other studies (Tang et al., 2010; Niwa et al., 2012; Tang and Xia, 2013) but not in a manner that correlates with disease severity.
evidence: This is based on comparison of multiple cited studies.

claim: R155H is a weak disease mutation in patients, with only a modest impact on the NTD up/down equilibrium, yet R155H p97 has been reported to have a particularly high ATPase activity and a low affinity for ADP.
source: Further, R155H is a weak disease mutation in patients (Mehta et al., 2013), with only a modest impact on the NTD up/down equilibrium, yet R155H p97 has been reported to have a particularly high ATPase activity and a low affinity for ADP (Tang and Xia, 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Mehta et al., 2013 and Tang and Xia, 2013.

claim: Perturbation of the up/down NTD equilibrium in the p97-ADP state due to mutation couples to disease by impairing p97 binding to the UBXD1 adaptor.
source: In contrast, our results provide strong support for a model whereby perturbation of the up/down NTD equilibrium in the p97-ADP state due to mutation couples to disease by impairing p97 binding to the UBXD1 adaptor.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by NMR binding data.

claim: Stronger perturbations to the NTD equilibrium lead to more acute disease.
source: Stronger perturbations lead to more acute disease (Figure 10).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 10.

claim: The binding of other adaptors, such as p47, that are involved in processes distinct from that of UBXD1, are much less affected, if at all, by the IBMPFD mutations.
source: The binding of other adaptors, such as p47, that are involved in processes distinct from that of UBXD1, are much less affected, if at all, by the IBMPFD mutations.
evidence: This is supported by NMR binding data comparing p47 and UBXD1.

claim: The key conclusions about the disease mutants can be obtained without extensive assignment, by recording simple 2D 13C-1H HMQC spectra of the IBMPFD mutant series.
source: While we report near-complete methyl group assignments for both ADP and ATP states of ND1Lp97 it is worth mentioning that the key conclusions about the disease mutants can be obtained without extensive assignment, by recording simple 2D 13C-1H HMQC spectra of the IBMPFD mutant series, with quantification of the NTD up/down populations from the CSPs of only a few key reporter residues.
evidence: This is a methodological observation based on the data presented.

claim: The primary effect of disease causing mutations is a change in NTD dynamics accompanied by more subtle structural changes that propagate to regions distal from the sites of mutation.
source: Our NMR results paint a picture whereby the primary effect of disease causing mutations is a change in NTD dynamics accompanied by more subtle structural changes that propagate to regions distal from the sites of mutation.
evidence: This is a primary conclusion supported by NMR data.

claim: Perturbations to the up/down NTD equilibrium are observed in the form of CSPs that extend across the NTD/D1 interface and include the linker region, which in turn connects to the nucleotide-binding site.
source: Perturbations to the up/down NTD equilibrium are observed in the form of CSPs that extend across the NTD/D1 interface and include the linker region, which in turn connects to the nucleotide-binding site (Figure 9).
evidence: This is supported by NMR data shown in Figure 9.

claim: Many of the 22 mutation sites reported to date in ND1Lp97 are localized to regions with large CSPs, suggesting that these loci serve as 'hot-spots' for propagation of conformational changes.
source: Indeed, many of the 22 mutation sites reported to date in ND1Lp97 are localized to regions with large CSPs, suggesting that these loci serve as 'hot-spots' for propagation of conformational changes.
evidence: This is inferred from NMR data showing CSPs at mutation sites.

claim: These hot-spot sites may well serve as starting points for the rational design of drug molecules that modulate NTD-D1 interactions.
source: Such sites may well serve as starting points for the rational design of drug molecules that modulate NTD-D1 interactions, potentially reversing the effects of the disease mutations or inhibiting the wt protein, a strategy currently explored in clinical cancer studies (Anderson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation about potential applications supported by citation to Anderson et al., 2015.

claim: R155H and R155C are the two most frequent mutations in patients.
source: An important result from this study is the strong correlation between disease severity and the extent to which the up/down equilibrium is skewed in the ND1Lp97-ADP state with more severe mutants unable to engage the H1/H2 region of UBXD1 that is required to lock the NTD conformation in the down state, illustrated schematically in Figure 10B. Because a complex of UBXD1-p97 is required for recruitment of ubiquitylated caveolin-1 to the lysosome for degradation this pathway becomes impaired in the disease mutants, leading to the accumulation of caveolin-1 positive endolysosomes in IBMPFD patients (Ritz et al., 2011). Notably, significantly impaired binding to IBMPFD disease mutants of p97 is not observed for all adaptors. For example, we have shown that binding of p47 is not perturbed by mutation (see below), consistent with the location of observed CSPs showing that p47-p97 interactions only engage the NTD and do not include the NTD-D1 interface, as for UBXD1 (compare Figure 7E and Figure 8B).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mehta et al., 2013.

claim: R155C is associated with a significantly earlier onset of symptoms compared to R155H and showed significantly reduced mean survival.
source: Disease (PDB=Paget disease of bone, IBM=inclusion body myopathy, FTD=frontotemporal dementia) onset and elevation of biochemical markers relative to normal (ALP=alkaline phosphatase, PYD=pyridinoline, DPD=deoxypyridinoline) (Mehta et al., 2013), is correlated with the extent of perturbation of the NTD up/down equilibrium. Data from R155H (R155C/P, R95G) patients are used for 'weak' ('strong') mutants; R155C is associated with a significantly earlier onset of symptoms compared to R155H and showed significantly reduced mean survival (Mehta et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Mehta et al., 2013.

claim: A complex of UBXD1-p97 is required for recruitment of ubiquitylated caveolin-1 to the lysosome for degradation.
source: Because a complex of UBXD1-p97 is required for recruitment of ubiquitylated caveolin-1 to the lysosome for degradation this pathway becomes impaired in the disease mutants, leading to the accumulation of caveolin-1 positive endolysosomes in IBMPFD patients (Ritz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ritz et al., 2011.

claim: This pathway becomes impaired in the disease mutants, leading to the accumulation of caveolin-1 positive endolysosomes in IBMPFD patients.
source: Because a complex of UBXD1-p97 is required for recruitment of ubiquitylated caveolin-1 to the lysosome for degradation this pathway becomes impaired in the disease mutants, leading to the accumulation of caveolin-1 positive endolysosomes in IBMPFD patients (Ritz et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Ritz et al., 2011.
